entry.title: LoRA on a 16 GB card: what fits and what does not
entry.summary: A 7B model is the honest ceiling for LoRA fine-tuning on a 16 GB consumer card, not because anything bigger throws an error, but because a 14B model silently spills into system memory and runs 50 times slower without ever reporting a failure. Key takeaways 7B is the real ceiling on an RTX 5070 Ti at LoRA rank 16, sequence length 512, batch size 1: 11,897.9 MiB peak, well inside the card's 16,303 MiB. 14B completed without a raised exception in both tested conditions, but peak VRAM read 22,189.8 MiB (136% of the card) and 17,470.9 MiB (107%) - both over the physical limit, through Windows' silent system-memory fallback. The cost of that fallback is severe: 21.7 seconds per training step at 14B against 0.4 seconds at 7B, roughly 51 times slower, with no error message anywhere. Gradient check…

entry.title: I built a free WCAG 2.2 checker that's honest about what automated scans miss
entry.summary: Agencies get asked "is our site accessible?" all the time. Most answers are either vague ("we follow WCAG") or a five-figure manual audit. I built something in between: A11yKeeper — paste a URL, it runs axe-core across that page plus up to 9 linked pages (~1 min), groups issues by severity, and gives a plain-English fix for each. It says clearly that a clean scan ≠ accessible. Deque's 2021 data puts automated detection at ~57% of issues by volume; every report ends with what a human still has to check (keyboard, screen reader, content). No overlay, nothing injected into your site. 3 free scans/day, no signup to see results. Agencies can put their own name on a white-label PDF for clients. On the W3C's deliberately broken demo site it found 353 issues across 10 pages. I'm looking for 5 founding agencies to shape scheduled re-checks and read-only client links — 50% off for as long as they stay subscribed. Would love feedback on false positives or confusing fix text: https://a11ykeeper.com Independent developer. Not a compliance certificate — a triage list.

entry.title: Why I pre-register a kill-gate for every experiment
entry.summary: A kill-gate is a threshold written down before an experiment runs: if the result crosses it, the idea dies. The writing down happens first, because after the numbers arrive, every threshold becomes negotiable. Last week two of my gates fired and one refused to answer, which taught me more than a success would have. Key takeaways A kill-gate names, in advance, the number at which I abandon my own hypothesis; the plan file is frozen before the first run and never rewritten afterwards. Gates exist because results negotiate: search-time contamination alone can inflate agent benchmark scores by up to 4%, and LLM-judge scores now come with conformal prediction intervals because point values wobble. entry.summary: A push notification to your phone is the simplest way to know what an Expert Advisor is doing while you are away from the terminal. Executive Problem Statement
Industrial automation teams and robotics companies are burning thousands of dollars monthly hosting high-VRAM GPU cloud nodes just to visualize and infer physical environments in real time.
